ledger.claim: A device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale.
ledger.request_basis: a device is not fully owned when its maker can disable features after sale

sentences.text: A device you’ve bought can still have a boss.

If its maker can disable features after sale, then your purchase came with a power attached to it – a power that remains on the other side of the transaction, waiting to decide what your thing is allowed to do.
That isn’t full ownership.
We usually talk about ownership as if it were a simple handoff: you give someone money, and they give you the object.
After that, you can use it, repair it, lend it, sell it, or leave it in a drawer until the battery dies of old age.
The seller’s role is finished (or so the story goes).
But a device whose capabilities can be withdrawn isn’t merely an object in your possession; it’s an object plus a continuing permission slip.
The permission slip can be revoked.
What does it mean to own a tool if someone else can reach through the network and remove the tool you paid for?
What does it mean to own a car, camera, appliance, or phone if the important part of its function depends on a decision made after your money has changed hands?
You may possess the shell, the screen, the motor, and the little screws, but possession of the physical parts isn’t the same thing as control of the device.
That distinction is the whole fight.
The familiar reply is that the maker needs this power for safety, maintenance, compatibility, or some other respectable purpose.
I think those purposes can be real without making the underlying arrangement acceptable.
A manufacturer may need to correct a defect; it doesn’t follow that it should be able to turn a purchased capability into a subscription by remote command.
A service may need updates; it doesn’t follow that the buyer should lose the old function when the service provider changes its mind.
The exception has swallowed the rule.
Notice what has happened to the word “buy.”
It now does two jobs at once: it describes the transfer of money and it disguises the retention of control.
You’re told that you own the device, while the maker keeps a veto over what the device can do.
That’s not a minor technical qualification (the sort of footnote you can ignore while admiring the shiny product).
It’s the central term of the bargain.
We should be especially suspicious of ownership that works only while another party remains cooperative.
If your neighbor can switch off your bicycle, you don’t call the bicycle fully yours; you call it borrowed under unusually aggressive supervision.
If a landlord could enter your kitchen and remove the oven whenever it wanted, the lease would still say “home,” but the word would be doing some pretty dishonest work.
A remotely disabled device is the digital version of that trick – a sale that preserves the seller’s hand on the controls.
This matters because the loss isn’t limited to one feature.

Once the maker can withdraw functionality, it can shape your choices after the sale: which repairs seem worthwhile, which accessories remain useful, which uses are permitted, and when replacement becomes unavoidable.
You’ve paid for an object, but you’re still negotiating with its owner.
And that owner isn’t you.
The policy question, then, isn’t whether devices should ever change.
Of course they’ll change.
The question is whether change can be imposed as a condition of continued use after the buyer has already paid.
We can require clear limits before purchase, preserve meaningful offline operation, protect repair and resale, and forbid the maker from silently converting ownership into revocable access.
Those rules wouldn’t freeze technology; they’d put the buyer back inside the definition of buying.
Don’t let the network connection become a hidden leash.
If a maker can disable what you bought, then you bought access to a device, not the device itself.
That’s a hell of a distinction to discover after the receipt is in your hand.
